_why: Which model to run, by what your machine has. Separate from engines.json on purpose: that file holds PROVIDER facts (how to talk to a server), this one holds MODEL judgement (which weights to load). A provider row is config; a model row is a claim about quality, and a claim needs evidence.
_status_rule: Every entry is `measured` or `available`, and the distinction is the point. `measured` means it ran the 40-key stress corpus through this tool and the numbers below are its own. `available` means the GGUF exists and the family looks promising — nothing more. A larger sibling of a winner is a CANDIDATE, never a recommendation: TranslateGemma proved it, where the 4B lost a brand name and dropped a key while its 12B sibling looked flawless — and then the 12B itself failed structurally once re-measured cleanly. Promote a row by running it, not by reasoning about it.
_measurement_discipline: MEASURED 2026-07-28, and the discipline is what makes the numbers usable: every resident model is unloaded (POST /api/generate {keep_alive:0}) before each run and runs are strictly sequential. A timing taken while another engine may hold VRAM is NOT a measurement — Hy-MT2-7B read 232.6 s on 2026-07-27 under contention and 36.6 s clean, 6.4x apart, on a model small enough that it never leaves the card. The earlier 2026-07-27 figures in git history were all taken without this discipline and on RAM running at 2133 MT/s instead of its rated 3600; both effects are corrected here.
_how_scored: REAL ERRORS, not the raw flag count — the flagged strings were read rather than tallied, and the count lied in both directions. `· {n} tokens` is flagged `untranslated` on every model that correctly left it alone (a false positive that penalises the right answer), while Hy-MT2 escaped that flag only by rewriting it to `· Tokens {n}`, reordering and capitalising for no reason — the check REWARDED the worse output. The flagship's one `numbers` flag did not reproduce on a second run: sampling noise. So `result` below gives structural failures (always disqualifying) and real errors after reading, with the raw flag count only where it differs interestingly.
_size_does_not_predict_fit: Measured on an 8 GB card: gemma3:12b and translategemma:12b are BOTH 8.1 GB on disk; measured cleanly they took 166.7 s and 366.2 s for the same 40 keys, and the second one FAILED structurally (2 keys exhausted every retry). Disk size tells you almost nothing about whether a model is usable; architecture, context and offload behaviour decide it. The clearest case is the 26B-A4B MoE: at ~15 GB it is the largest thing here and also among the fastest, because only ~4B parameters are active per token.
_the_corpus: 40 keys chosen to break things: all 8 plural-pipe forms, 20 interpolations, 10 long paragraphs with named slots, 7 glossary keys, 15 short labels. Structural = placeholders/plurals/glossary/missing. Semantic = the checks only Layer 2 sees, chiefly the Spanish opening ¿.

8gb._measured_on: RTX 2070 Super, 8 GB VRAM, 32 GB system RAM at its rated 3600 MT/s, Ollama, 2026-07-28. Note that VRAM is not the only constraint — the MoE below is a ~15 GB download that runs here by offloading, so disk and system RAM decide whether you can use it at all.

recommended.result: 0 structural failures, 1 semantic flag, ZERO real errors after reading; 166.7 s for the corpus
recommended.why: the right pick for a machine that cannot hold the flagship. It is NOT the most accurate or the fastest model measured — the 26B-A4B MoE beats it on both — but that one is a ~15 GB download, and availability is not a recommendation. gemma3:12b finishes with zero real errors at a size that fits an 8 GB card, including 0/5 misses on the Spanish opening ¿ across every run it has had.

alternatives.model: gemma-4-26b-a4b-qat (Gemma-4 26B-A4B QAT GGUF, served by Ollama or llama-server)
alternatives.result: 0 structural failures, ZERO real errors, in THREE placements: GPU offload 73.8 s (retest 74.2 s), genuinely CPU-only 128.8 s, Ollama num_gpu:0 132.0 s (retest 131.9 s)
alternatives.why: the most accurate thing measured here, and faster than the 8 GB default even when it runs on the CPU alone — 26B with only ~4B active is what a MoE is for. Not the recommendation only because of the ~15 GB download. Two practical notes: it is a THINKING model, so it returns empty content until you set `think: false` in your config (the ollama profile deliberately sends no think field); and running it entirely on CPU leaves the card completely free, which on this machine still beat the default running WITH GPU offload.
alternatives.pull: not a public Ollama tag — supply your own Gemma-4 26B-A4B QAT GGUF and set `model` (and `think: false`) in your config

alternatives.result: 0 structural failures, 3 semantic flags, 2-3 REAL errors; 36.6 s (retest 37.8 s) — by far the fastest
alternatives.why: the speed option, and it costs correctness. It misses the Spanish opening ¿ on the same key on BOTH runs — the identical reproducible failure that disqualified qwen3:8b, with the rule in the same system prompt, so it is a model property and not prompt-fixable — and one run invented the noun `proyectos` in an otherwise fluent sentence, dropping a closing parenthesis with it. Twice as fast as the flagship and the least accurate model that finished. Reasonable if you will review the output with --probe and the review page; wrong if you plan to ship it unread.

alternatives.result: 0 structural failures; misses the opening ¿ (1 of 5, then 5 of 5 on a second run) plus three genuinely untranslated keys; 111.1 s measured cleanly
alternatives.why: the cautionary tale that started the structural/semantic split: it passes every structural check and is measurably unreliable on Spanish punctuation — unreliable rather than simply wrong, which is worse to plan around. Superseded on every axis by Hy-MT2-7B (faster, smaller) and gemma3:12b (accurate).

avoid.result: DISQUALIFIED — 38/40 keys, 2 keys exhausted every retry (`missing`, a structural failure), 23 requests of retry-and-split, 366.2 s
avoid.why: it had been the only local model with zero flags of any kind, rejected solely on a 1,145 s runtime — and that result does not reproduce. Measured cleanly it fails structurally. Worth keeping in the file as the reason `measured` means measured RECENTLY and under controlled conditions: a good result taken under contention is not evidence.

avoid.result: 39/40 keys, translated the do-not-translate brand `Strands` to `Hilos`, lost a plural pipe
avoid.why: the specialised-model trap. Translation-tuned, and at 4B it lacks the instruction-following to honour a glossary — it faithfully translates the thing you told it not to.

4gb_and_under._note: Nothing here is measured. The only small model tested at all, translategemma:4b, FAILED — so this tier has no recommendation rather than a guess. Use a cloud engine instead if this is your hardware. Candidates worth running: Hy-MT2-1.8B (first-party Tencent GGUF) and gemma3:4b — but note that the 7B of that same family already misses the Spanish ¿ reproducibly, so expect the 1.8B to need review.

16gb._note: No 16 GB card here, so nothing is measured ON one. The evidence-backed reasoning: the 26B-A4B MoE already ran clean with zero real errors at 73.8 s while OFFLOADING on an 8 GB card, so a 16 GB card can only help it — that is the first thing to try, and a measured run would likely make it this tier's recommendation.

candidates.why: measured clean on 8 GB via offload (see the 8gb tier); more VRAM removes the offload penalty. Needs think:false.
first-party Tencent GGUF, a 30B MoE with ~3B active. Caveat from measurement: the 7B of this family has a reproducible Spanish ¿ failure, so verify that before trusting the family.
larger sibling of the model that is clean at 8 GB.

24gb_plus._note: Untested. Listed so users with the hardware know where to look, explicitly NOT as recommendations.

candidates.why: the same MoE at a higher quant.
Unbabel's translation-specialist family at its largest. Note the GGUFs are third-party quants; the first-party release is safetensors.

cloud.result: 40/40, 0 structural, 0 semantic, 94 s — the best quality-per-second measured here (2026-07-27; not re-measured in the clean 2026-07-28 set, because one corpus run is 3 of the 20 daily requests)
cloud.why: and unusable for real work: the free tier is 20 requests per DAY per model. One 846-key catalogue is 36 requests. Use it to prove a config, not to translate a product. A paid tier or `openai` removes the limit and the reasoning above stops applying.
